{{Short description|Generalization of the mathematical factorial}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Bhargava's factorial function''', or simply the '''Bhargava factorial''', is a generalization of the [[factorial]] function developed by [[Manjul Bhargava]] as part of his bachelor's thesis at [[Harvard University]] in 1996. Bhargava subsequently published a revised version in ''[[The American Mathematical Monthly]]'' in 2000. The Bhargava factorial has the property that many [[number theory|number-theoretic]] results involving the ordinary factorials remain true even when the factorials are replaced by the Bhargava factorials. Using an arbitrary [[infinite set|infinite subset]] ''S'' of the set <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> of integers, Bhargava associated a positive integer with every positive integer ''k'', which he denoted by ''k'' !<sub>''S''</sub>, with the property that if one takes ''S'' = <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> itself, then the integer associated with ''k'', that is ''k'' !<sub><math>\mathbb{Z}</math> </sub>, would turn out to be the ordinary factorial of ''k''.<ref name=MAA>{{cite journal
| last = Bhargava
| first = Manjul
| url = http://www.maa.org/sites/default/files/pdf/upload_library/22/Hasse/00029890.di021346.02p0064l.pdf
| title = The Factorial Function and Generalizations
| journal = The American Mathematical Monthly
| volume = 107
| year = 2000
| pages = 783–799
| doi = 10.2307/2695734
| issue = 9
| jstor = 2695734
| citeseerx = 10.1.1.585.2265
}}</ref>

==Motivation for the generalization==
The [[factorial]] of a [[non-negative integer]] ''n'', denoted by ''n''!, is the product of all positive integers less than or equal to ''n''. For example, 5! = 5×4×3×2×1 = 120. By convention, the value of 0! is defined as 1. This  classical factorial function appears prominently in many theorems in [[number theory]]. The following are a few of these theorems.<ref name=MAA/>

# For any positive integers ''m'' and ''n'', (''m'' + ''n'')! is a multiple of ''m''! ''n''!.
# Let ''f''(''x'') be a primitive [[integer polynomial]], that is, a polynomial in which the coefficients are integers and are [[relatively prime]] to each other. If the degree of ''f''(''x'') is ''k'' then the [[greatest common divisor]] of the set of values of ''f''(''x'') for integer values of ''x'' is a [[divisor]] of ''k''!.
# Let ''a''<sub>0</sub>, ''a''<sub>1</sub>, ''a''<sub>2</sub>, ... , ''a''<sub>''n''</sub> be any ''n'' + 1 integers. Then the product of their pairwise differences is a multiple of 0! 1! ... ''n''!.
# Let <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> be the set of integers and ''n'' any integer. Then the number of [[polynomial function]]s from the [[ring of integers]] <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>  to the [[quotient ring]]  <math>\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}</math> is given by <math>\prod_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{n}{\gcd(n,k!)}</math>.

Bhargava posed to himself the following problem and obtained an affirmative answer: In the above theorems, can one replace the set of integers by some other set ''S'' (a subset of <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>, or a subset of some [[Ring (mathematics)|ring]]) and define a function depending on ''S'' which assigns a value to each non-negative integer ''k'', denoted by ''k''!<sub>''S''</sub>, such that the statements obtained from the theorems given earlier by replacing ''k''! by ''k''!<sub>''S''</sub> remain true?

==The generalisation==

* Let ''S'' be an arbitrary infinite subset of the set ''Z'' of integers.
* Choose a prime number ''p''.
* Construct an ordered sequence {''a''<sub>0</sub>, ''a''<sub>1</sub>, ''a''<sub>2</sub>, ... } of numbers chosen from ''S'' as follows (such a sequence is called a ''p''-ordering of ''S''):
:# ''a''<sub>0</sub> is any arbitrary element of ''S''.
:# ''a''<sub>1</sub> is any arbitrary element of ''S'' such that the highest power of ''p'' that divides ''a''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>0</sub> is minimum.
:# ''a''<sub>2</sub> is any arbitrary element of ''S'' such that the highest power of ''p'' that divides (''a''<sub>2</sub>&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>0</sub>)(''a''<sub>2</sub>&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>1</sub>) is minimum.
:# ''a''<sub>3</sub> is any arbitrary element of ''S'' such that the highest power of ''p'' that divides (''a''<sub>3</sub>&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>0</sub>)(''a''<sub>3</sub>&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>1</sub>)(''a''<sub>3</sub>&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>2</sub>) is minimum.
:# ... and so on.
* Construct a ''p''-ordering of ''S'' for each prime number ''p''. (For a given prime number ''p'', the ''p''-ordering of ''S'' is not unique.)
* For each non-negative integer ''k'', let ''v''<sub>''k''</sub>(''S'', ''p'') be the highest power of ''p'' that divides (''a''<sub>''k''</sub>&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>0</sub>)(''a''<sub>''k''</sub>&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>1</sub>)(''a''<sub>''k''</sub>&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>2</sub>) ... (''a''<sub>''k''</sub>&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>''k''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1</sub>). The sequence {''v''<sub>0</sub>(''S'', ''p''), ''v''<sub>1</sub>(''S'', ''p''), ''v''<sub>2</sub>(''S'', ''p''), ''v''<sub>3</sub>(''S'', ''p''), ... } is called the associated ''p''-sequence of ''S''. This is independent of any particular choice of ''p''-ordering of ''S''. (We assume that ''v''<sub>0</sub>(''S'', ''p'') = 1 always.)
* The factorial of the integer ''k'', associated with the infinite set ''S'', is defined as <math>k!_{S}=\prod_p v_k(S,p)</math>, where the product is taken over all prime numbers ''p''.

==Example: Factorials using set of prime numbers==

Let ''S'' be the set of all prime numbers ''P'' = {2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ... }.
:* Choose ''p'' = 2 and form a ''p''-ordering of ''P''.
::* Choose ''a''<sub>0</sub> = 19 arbitrarily from ''P''.
::* To choose ''a''<sub>1</sub>:
:::* The highest power of ''p'' that divides 2&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>0</sub> = −17 is 2<sup>0</sup> = 1. Also, for any ''a'' ≠ 2 in P, ''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>0</sub> is divisible by 2. Hence, the highest power of ''p'' that divides (''a''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>0</sub>) is minimum when ''a''<sub>1</sub> = 2 and the minimum power is 1. Thus ''a''<sub>1</sub> is chosen as 2 and ''v''<sub>1</sub>(''P'', 2) = 1.
::* To choose ''a''<sub>2</sub>:
:::* It can be seen that for each element ''a'' in ''P'', the product ''x'' = (''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>0</sub>)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>1</sub>) = (''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;19)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;2) is divisible by 2. Also, when ''a'' = 5, ''x'' is divisible 2  and it is not divisible by any higher power of 2. So, ''a''<sub>2</sub> may be chosen as 5. We have ''v''<sub>2</sub>(''P'', 2) = 2.
::* To choose ''a''<sub>3</sub>:
:::* It can be seen that for each element ''a'' in ''P'', the product ''x'' = (''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>0</sub>)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>1</sub>)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>2</sub>) = (''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;19)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;2)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;5) is divisible by 2<sup>3</sup> = 8. Also, when ''a'' = 17, ''x'' is divisible by 8  and it is not divisible by any higher power of 2. Choose ''a''<sub>3</sub> = 17. Also we have ''v''<sub>3</sub>(''P'',2) = 8.
::* To choose ''a''<sub>4</sub>:
:::* It can be seen that for each element ''a'' in ''P'', the product ''x'' = (''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>0</sub>)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>1</sub>)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>2</sub>)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>3</sub>) = (''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;19)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;2)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;5)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;17) is divisible by 2<sup>4</sup> = 16. Also, when ''a'' = 23, ''x'' is divisible 16  and it is not divisible by any higher power of 2. Choose ''a''<sub>4</sub> = 23. Also we have ''v''<sub>4</sub>(''P'',2) = 16.
::* To choose ''a''<sub>5</sub>:
:::* It can be seen that for each element ''a'' in ''P'', the product ''x'' = (''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>0</sub>)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>1</sub>)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>2</sub>)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>3</sub>)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''a''<sub>4</sub>) = (''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;19)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;2)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;5)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;17)(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;23) is divisible by 2<sup>7</sup> = 128. Also, when ''a'' = 31, ''x'' is divisible 128  and it is not divisible by any higher power of 2. Choose ''a''<sub>5</sub> = 31. Also we have ''v''<sub>5</sub>(''P'',2) = 128.
::* The process is continued. Thus a 2-ordering of P is {19, 2, 5, 17, 23, 31, ... } and the associated 2-sequence is {1, 1, 2, 8, 16, 128, ... }, assuming that ''v''<sub>0</sub>(''P'', 2) = 1.

:* For ''p'' = 3, one possible ''p''-ordering of ''P'' is the sequence {2, 3, 7, 5, 13, 17, 19, ... } and the associated ''p''-sequence of ''P'' is {1, 1, 1, 3, 3, 9, ... }.

:* For ''p'' = 5, one possible ''p''-ordering of ''P'' is the sequence {2, 3, 5, 19, 11, 7, 13, ... } and the associated ''p''-sequence is  {1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 5, ...}.

:* It can be shown that for ''p'' ≥ 7, the first few elements of the associated ''p''-sequences are {1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1,  ... }.

==Example: Factorials using the set of natural numbers==

Let ''S'' be the set of integers <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>.

:* For ''p'' = 2, the associated ''p''-sequence is {1, 1, 2, 2, 8, 8, 16, 16, 128, 128, 256, 256, ... }.
:* For ''p'' = 3, the associated ''p''-sequence is {1, 1, 1, 3, 3, 3, 9, 9, 9, 27, 27, 27, 81, 81, 81, ... }.
:* For ''p'' = 5, the associated ''p''-sequence is {1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 25, 25, 25, 25, 25, ... }.
:* For ''p'' = 7, the associated ''p''-sequence is {1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7, ... }.
:* ... and so on.

Thus the first few factorials using the integers are

:* 0!<sub><math>\mathbb{Z}</math></sub> = 1×1×1×1×1×... = 1.
:* 1!<sub><math>\mathbb{Z}</math></sub> = 1×1×1×1×1×... = 1.
:* 2!<sub><math>\mathbb{Z}</math></sub> = 2×1×1×1×1×... = 2.
:* 3!<sub><math>\mathbb{Z}</math></sub> = 2×3×1×1×1×... = 6.
:* 4!<sub><math>\mathbb{Z}</math></sub> = 8×3×1×1×1×... = 24.
:* 5!<sub><math>\mathbb{Z}</math></sub> = 8×3×5×1×1×... = 120.
:* 6!<sub><math>\mathbb{Z}</math></sub> = 16×9×5×1×1×... = 720.

The following table contains the general expressions for ''k''!<sub>''S''</sub> for some special cases of ''S''.<ref name=MAA/>

| 1 || Set of integers || ''k''!
|-

|-
| 3 || Set of integers of the form ''an'' + ''b'' || ''a''<sup>''k''</sup>×''k''!
|-
| 4 || Set of integers of the form 2<sup>''n''</sup> || (2<sup>''k''</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;1)(2<sup>''k''</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;2) ... (2<sup>''k''</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;2<sup>''k''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1</sup>)
|-
| 5 || Set of integers of the form ''q''<sup>''n''</sup> for some prime ''q''|| (''q''<sup>''k''</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;1)(''q''<sup>''k''</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;''q'') ... (''q''<sup>''k''</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;''q''<sup>''k''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1</sup>)
|-
| 6 || Set of squares of integers || (2''k'')!/2
|}
